assets.content:
Subject: How a testimonial request gets built in Senja
Preview text: Write the questions, set each to text, video or a rating, switch on follow-ups, then open the page yourself.

Hi there,

Senja collects text and video testimonials, and the student's side of it is one page you build yourself first.

In a free account you write the questions you want to put to your cohort and set each one to text, video or a rating. A whole form can be limited to video only, or to text only.

What your student opens is a personalised page. They write or record their answer there, with no account and no special software — Senja describes that as taking about 30 seconds.

Worth knowing before you send it: every question you show has to be answered, there's no optional question yet, and their name is always required.

Then the chasing is a switch rather than a habit. Turn follow-ups on and Senja sends up to three reminder emails, 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite, only to students who haven't responded. Three is the maximum.

Build it, open the page from your student's side, and decide then whether it's a request you'd be comfortable sending.

Build your form on a free account → https://app.senja.io/signup

- Senja, Support & Ops

P.S. Free collects 15 text and video testimonials; past that, new ones stay hidden until you upgrade.

brief.promise: Asking your students for a testimonial has a known, bounded shape — one form you build, a page they open without an account, follow-ups capped at three — and you can build the whole thing on a free account and look at it before you send anything.
brief.orientation: For a small course or coaching team collecting student feedback for course and cohort sales pages, Senja is a tool for requesting text or video testimonials and displaying or reusing the responses.
brief.arc: One email, so there is no arc across slots — the whole argument has to land cold and stand alone. It moves in one turn: name the part this reader hasn't settled (the ask), replace "a message I have to write and then keep chasing" with a documented setup — a form, a student-facing page, a reminder schedule that stops after three — and end on the one step that lets them inspect that setup for themselves on a free account. The email argues about the request, never about what the request will produce.
brief.sequence_rationale: One email was requested in so many words, so the only real decision was which single argument to spend it on. The display/reuse shelf (embeds, hosting, reels) is bigger, but this reader is solution-aware: they already agree testimonials belong on the cohort page. The grounded uncertainty in the research sits upstream of that, on the ask — P1 (doesn't know how to get them, doesn't want to seem pushy) and P2's format-and-where question. So the email argues the mechanism of asking and leaves the display argument as the alternative bet rather than crowding both in. The previous version of this brief failed on scope, not on choice of shelf: its promise and belief shift implied an outcome of asking (better recollections, a request students receive well) that the evidence cannot carry. The repair keeps the shelf and rebuilds the claim one level lower, on the request itself — what the creator builds, what the student is asked to do, how far the reminders go — which is exactly what the assigned facts document and what the free next step actually shows. Evidence is three facts a stranger can check rather than four that would turn it into a feature list: E150 for the form the creator builds, R3 for what lands on the student's side, E27 for the bounded follow-up schedule that answers the real hesitation. Dropped P3 entirely: its only usable payoff would have been that prompter asking produces stronger testimonials, which is forbidden, so keeping it as a premise invited the same drift again. On the objection: the supported hesitation is this reader's reluctance to make an open-ended demand of people who already paid, and it has a supported answer in the documented size and boundedness of the request. It has no supported answer about how students will react, so that half stays out and is written into must_not_say instead. There is no verified objection list for this audience ("why they say no: not established"), so the objection is derived from P1's grounded wording and held to what the assigned evidence can answer.

emails.selection_reason: The grounded problems for this slice are about the request, not the display: a creator who doesn't know how to get testimonials and is reluctant to ask in case it seems pushy (P1), and who is unsure whether to ask for video or writing and where to collect it (P2). The dossier links both to the collection-form and invite evidence, and those facts are the kind a cold reader can check in one line each — a form you build yourself, a student page that needs no account and takes text or video, follow-ups capped at three on a fixed schedule. That makes the request the one place this product's documented mechanism meets this reader's open question, and the free account is where they can see the request before committing to send it.
emails.argument_issue: Both fits are PARTIAL, and that sets the ceiling for this email. The assigned evidence establishes how the creator builds and sends the request, what the student is asked to do and how many reminders can follow. It does not establish that students will respond, that they will find being asked reasonable, which format persuades prospective students, or that anything about timing improves what gets written. The claim is therefore confined to the documented shape and cost of the request, and the next step is confined to seeing that request — not to any result from sending it.
emails.job: Get a cohort-based course operator to create a free Senja account and build the student testimonial request they have been meaning to figure out, so they can see exactly what it asks of their students before sending it.
emails.single_idea: Asking students for a testimonial is a setup job, not a correspondence job: you build one form, your student answers it on a page with no account and no software, and the follow-ups are capped — three emails on a fixed schedule you switch on once, only to people who haven't answered.

The same creator is unsure whether incentives would seem fake, whether to request video or written testimonials, and where to collect and display them.
emails.mechanism: The request stops being correspondence and becomes a form. In a Senja account you build a collection form — simple or multistep; Senja says 60 seconds — and you decide per question whether a student writes or records, so the video-or-written question becomes a setting instead of a dilemma. What lands on your student's side is a personalised page: they write or record their answer there, with no account and no special software, and Senja describes that as taking about 30 seconds. Then the chasing is a switch rather than a habit: turn follow-ups on and Senja sends up to three reminder emails, 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, only to students who haven't responded. The thing you set once is the schedule; nothing here says how students will answer it.

must_not_say: Do not promise or imply any outcome of sending the request: no reply rates, no 'you'll have testimonials by Friday', no claim that students will respond, and no claim that reminders produce submissions. Student reactions and response are explicitly not established.
Do not claim students will find the request reasonable, welcome it, or not feel nagged.
Do not promise that asking promptly, or reminding, produces stronger, more concrete or more detailed testimonials — the research records that belief, the evidence does not support the claim.
Do not say which format is better for persuading prospective students; text or video is a setting the reader chooses, not a recommendation this email can make.
No conversion, enrolment, sales or 'fills your cohort' claims.

Attribute both durations to their source and to the thing they describe: Senja says a simple or multistep form takes 60 seconds to create, and Senja describes its form as taking a customer about 30 seconds. Neither is a measured result with this reader's students, and neither describes how long the whole thing takes to roll out.

Do not say testimonials are collected 'on autopilot' or that requests fire when a student finishes a course: event-triggered auto-collect needs a connected platform and a paid plan, and neither is established for this reader. Do not name Teachable, Kajabi, Thinkific or any other platform as theirs.

Do not stretch the follow-up schedule: up to three emails, 1, 3 and 7 days after the original invite, to people who haven't responded — not an indefinite drip, and not retroactive to invites sent before follow-ups were switched on.
Do not claim reminders stop the moment a student submits; that behaviour is documented for the connected-platform auto-collect path, not for this one.
Do not imply unlimited free collection. Free is 15 video and text testimonials, and past that new ones are hidden until you upgrade.
Do not suggest students can skip questions: every displayed question is required, and so is their name.

Keep the display shelf out of this email — widget style names, Walls of Love, testimonial images, reels, the case study generator, Spin the Wheel, Thank Yous, the Chrome extension, Slack bot, MCP, Zapier, API, rich snippets, translation. One idea, and it is the ask.
Keep vendor-evaluation material out: refunds, seats, projects, custom domains, branding removal, competitor names and comparisons. Nobody here is choosing a vendor yet.
Do not use the 20,000-users figure as evidence that testimonials worked for anyone, or as proof of outcome.
Do not quote the buyer-vocabulary phrases as if they were customer testimonials; they are word choice, not attributed quotes.
Do not invent their cohort date, student numbers, a failed previous attempt, or a pile of proof sitting in a spreadsheet.

Keep the connection route attached to its cited source. A native or prebuilt integration and a custom HTTP/webhook endpoint are separate setup paths unless the source explicitly equates them. A platform name alone establishes neither manual endpoint configuration nor a no-setup connector. Keep unknown setup requirements unknown.
Forms and invitations provide a way to ask, but reduced reluctance, non-pushy reception and successful participation are not established by the selected evidence.
The product supplies format, collection and display options, but cannot establish which format is best or whether rewards will seem fake; one question cannot receive both text and video.
Event-triggered requests require a connected platform; current audience stack compatibility and stronger, more concrete recollections are not established by the selected evidence.
emails.objection: Asking students for a testimonial feels like an imposition — they already paid me, and I don't want to turn into the person sending reminder emails. (Answer it with the documented shape of the request: a page the student fills in with no account and no special software, text or video decided by the question you set, and follow-ups you switch on that are capped at three — 1, 3 and 7 days, only to people who haven't answered. Not with any claim about how students will feel or whether they will reply.)
emails.tone: Matter-of-fact and a little direct, with the smallest amount of sympathy for the thing they keep not doing. Short sentences, one idea per breath. No hype, no urgency they didn't earn, no swearing in a first cold email to a coach.
emails.next_step_decision: Whether this is a request they would actually be comfortable sending to their students — judged on the form they can build, the page their students would open, and how far the reminders go.
emails.next_step_value: A free account where they can build the collection form themselves — simple or multistep, with each question set to writing or video — open the page a student would see, where the student writes or records with no account and no special software, and switch on follow-ups, which are capped at three emails sent 1, 3 and 7 days after the invite to students who haven't responded.
emails.next_step_limit: Signing up shows them the request and its settings. It does not tell them how many students will reply, what students will make of being asked, whether writing or video suits their cohort, or what any of it does for enrolments — and it does not lift the Free plan's 15-testimonial limit or unlock the paid-only pieces (welcome videos, branding removal, auto-collect from connected platforms).
emails.subject_strategy: This reader is solution-aware: a subject that argues testimonials matter tells them something they already believe and gets archived. Earn the open on the part they haven't settled — what the ask actually consists of — with one concrete specific about the request itself (a form instead of a message, three reminders and then it stops, a page rather than a favour). Nothing about results, reply rates or a cohort deadline, and no question that can be answered 'yes, obviously'.

brief.voice_notes: Senja's own register: name the thing plainly before pitching the fix, short almost one-breath sentences, often one per paragraph, problem then turn then product — the way their case-study copy does it ('A good case study takes weeks of interviews and drafts, so most never get written. Senja builds one from a testimonial you already have.'). Their published voice will swear and will drop 'automagically'; neither belongs here — the first because this is a cold email to a coach, the second because this email must not imply testimonials arrive without anyone asking. Use their nouns (testimonials, social proof, form, invites) and the reader's own framing of the problem (asking, pushy, video or written) without quoting it as proof.
